To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 3 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 4 code files.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 308 columns across 3 data files.

Issues Identified

64 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet Formatting

We examined 3 spreadsheet files in the repository; 3 have at least one formatting issue.

File Sheet Issue Detail
raw_data_2022.xlsx Krieg in der Ukraine - Wahrnehm Empty or unnamed columns 15 columns are empty or have a blank header.
raw_data_2023.xlsx Krieg in der Ukraine - Wahrnehm Empty or unnamed columns 15 columns are empty or have a blank header.
raw_data_2025.xlsx Sheet1 Empty or unnamed columns 19 columns are empty or have a blank header.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script needs a file that another script should have made.

  • OSF_Analyses.qmd needs preprocessed_data_S1.RDa, which OSF_Preprocessing_Study1.R makes.

The other script stopped before it made the file, so fix that script first; this one may then run as well. To make the order clear to readers, number your scripts in the order they run (01_clean.R, 02_model.R), or add one main script that runs the others in order.

A script uses something it does not create or load itself.

  • OSF_Preprocessing_Study1.R: %>%
  • OSF_Preprocessing_Study2.R: %>%
  • OSF_Preprocessing_Study3.R: %>%

Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it.

  1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R).
  2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing.
  3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second.
  4. Load every package with library() at the top.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 4 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 OSF_Preprocessing_Study1.R — numeric
2 OSF_Preprocessing_Study2.R — numeric
3 OSF_Preprocessing_Study3.R — numeric
4 OSF_Analyses.qmd OSF_Preprocessing_Study1.R, OSF_Preprocessing_Study2.R, OSF_Preprocessing_Study3.R dependency

File paths

3 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: raw_data_2023.xlsx to ../Data/raw_data_2023.xlsx (in OSF_Preprocessing_Study2.R); raw_data_2025.xlsx to ../Data/raw_data_2025.xlsx (in OSF_Preprocessing_Study3.R); raw_data_2022.xlsx to ../Data/raw_data_2022.xlsx (in OSF_Preprocessing_Study1.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 0 ran without error, 4 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

a script hit a could not find function "..." error; we added the library() calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.

File Outcome Detail Time (s)

OSF_Preprocessing_Study2.R errored undefined_variable 1.4
OSF_Preprocessing_Study3.R errored undefined_variable 1.4
OSF_Analyses.qmd errored runtime 1.6

Undefined-variable errors

3 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function (object '...' not found / could not find function "..."). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper’s own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

File Missing variable Defined in
OSF_Preprocessing_Study1.R %>% (not defined anywhere in the paper’s code)
OSF_Preprocessing_Study2.R %>% (not defined anywhere in the paper’s code)
OSF_Preprocessing_Study3.R %>% (not defined anywhere in the paper’s code)

Calls that install packages in the code

12 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

library() calls added

4 scripts use functions from packages they do not load themselves. The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run them we added the library() calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after adding library() calls it should make itself.

File library() calls added
OSF_Preprocessing_Study1.R library(ggplot2)

OSF_Preprocessing_Study3.R library(ggplot2)

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

In total, we recruited 689 participants for the three waves (n2022 = 139, n2023 = 247, n2025 = 303) with a mean age of 35.84 (SD = 11.91).

Participants were recruited at three different time points.

All participants received information about the survey, the procedure, and gave written informed consent before participating.

After giving informed consent, participants provided demographic information.

Ethics approval statement:

All study waves complied with APA 7th ethical guidelines, the declaration of Helsinki, and were approved by the University of Salzburg Ethics Board (protocol no.

The present research complied with the American Psychological Association seventh ethical guidelines and was approved by the University of Salzburg Ethics Board, where the study was conducted.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
