General Discussion

From 2022 until 2025, we conducted a cross-sectional study with three measurement points to assess existential threat perceptions, collective responses, and associated emotional states to the war in Ukraine among European citizens. Across the four-year time span, we observed that the Ukrainian war was primarily perceived as a symbolic threat to core European values, and that defending the European ingroup by demonstrating unity, loyalty, and value defense was the most pronounced collective response over time. Regarding the underlying emotional processes, we found that anxiety, anger, and being moved were linked to both realistic and symbolic threat perceptions, but not to the threat of unpredictability.

Moreover, the emotional states predicted collective responses to a different degree. While negative emotions predicted the derogation of the outgroup of Russian citizens, positive and negative emotional states with approach-motivational tendencies, that is, anger and being moved, predicted solidarity with the Ukrainian outgroup and defense of the European ingroup. Interestingly, anxiety reduced ingroup defense, whereas feelings of being moved reduced support for derogatory expressions towards Russians and mistrust in mainstream media. Together, the findings support being moved and anger as predictors of (solidaritybased) collective action in times of crisis [10, 30, 36, 37]. Moreover, they show being moved as a collective approach emotion, which can strengthen the bond with one's ingroup, and which is strongly tied to the value of prosociality [33]. Notably, they show the first evidence that being moved can also help reduce outgroup derogation and mistrust in public mainstream media.

The Ukrainian war: A threat to realistic and symbolic concerns and to basic needs

Realistic concerns about the European economy and safety, but particularly the symbolic threat to European moral principles and basic values, such as a liberal democratic order, stood out over four years of war. In contrast, the unpredictability of the situation in Ukraine was perceived as low from the beginning in 2022 until 2025. This corroborates findings showing realistic and symbolic threats to play a role in long-term crises, such as the Covid-19 pandemic [1].

While the relative threat perceptions remained stable, changes over time could be observed regarding the absolute amount of perceived threat. Realistic and symbolic threat perceptions were highest directly after the invasion in 2022, then showing a slight decline. This is interesting because different aspects associated with the Ukrainian war received attention in each study wave. While in 2022 the military conflict and the associated humanitarian crisis were in focus, in 2023 economic consequences and inflation due to fossil fuel dependencies dominated the public impression in Europe. In 2025, peace negotiations and the future of European sovereignty came up as important issues. Despite this variance in the public discourse, the present findings suggest that, particularly, the intergroup nature of the conflict that was constantly salient influenced threat perceptions. European citizens in Germany and Austria perceived the Ukrainian war foremost as threat to their European identity. This adds to findings, showing symbolic threat perceptions caused by Western and Eastern identities play an important role in Slovaks' perceptions of the Ukrainian war [7, 8].

Here, perceived symbolic threat by Western identities (i.e., US, EU, Ukraine) predicted anti-Ukrainian prejudice [7], blaming Ukrainians for the war, and support for pro-Russian conspiracies [8].

An existential threat to basic human needs

In addition to realistic and symbolic threat perceptions, we observed that the Ukrainian war had an impact on individual need frustration. Comparing the violation of different basic needs showed that people were mostly bothered by uncontrollability, mortality, and uncertainty about their personal future. They perceived less influence over their lives, were reminded that they were mortal, and felt uncertain about their future and their place in the world. In contrast, their needs for meaning, self-esteem, belonging, and trust were less affected, with mean scores below the scale midpoint. This violation of basic individual needs qualifies the Ukrainian war as an individual existential threat to Europeans in Germany and Austria [3]. In a similar vein, threats to individual control and certainty have been observed during the Covid-19 pandemic as well [4, 20], and also during the global financial crisis in 2008 [19], underscoring the existentially threatening nature of large-scale crises.

Additionally, the recurrent measurement of basic need frustration allowed new insights into whether need frustration changed over time. For the Ukrainian war, we found that the reported amount of need frustration remained relatively stable from 2022 until 2025, yielding no remarkable changes (with an increase in belongingness frustration as an exception).

Together, the present findings point to the central role of the needs for control, certainty, and existence, which have been mostly and consistently affected by the Ukrainian war from 2022 until 2025. Future studies would benefit from measuring multiple need frustration, also together with realistic and symbolic threat perceptions, to better understand their importance and interrelations for societal crisis threats.

Collective responses from 2022 until 2025: From direct resolution to palliation

We measured different forms of collective threat responses [24], ranging from attempts to directly address the crisis and its consequences by helping Ukrainian refugees and protesting for peace, over indirect expressions to deal with the crisis by demonstrating agency of the European ingroup and defending its core values, to palliative responses of derogating people who ostensibly belonged to the Russian outgroup and mistrusting public media. At the beginning of the war in 2022, direct and indirect means to help Ukrainian refugees and to demonstrate agency through ingroup defense were more pronounced than palliative responses.

However, as the war lasted longer, palliative responses to mistrust public media (from 2022 to 2023), and to derogate Russian citizens (from 2022 to 2025) became more frequent. This points to the importance of investigating responses to enduring crises in the long run. It is possible that people initially respond to crisis threats by direct resolution attempts, while indirect means of ingroup support and defense, and even more so palliative responses that do not address the crisis itself, may primarily emerge when people notice that a solution is difficult to achieve. The present studies provide a first hint in this direction, but as they are cross-sectional, longitudinal designs are necessary to examine intraindividual changes in crisis responses.

Emotional states link threat perceptions to collective responses

Both realistic and symbolic threat perceptions were associated with heightened feelings of anger and being moved, while only realistic threat made people feel anxious. The intensity of emotional experience varied substantially across years, accounting for 11% variance of anxiety, 15% variance of anger, and 28% variance of being moved. This indicates that Europeans who lived in German-speaking countries showed a different emotional susceptibility from 2022 until 2025. Similar findings have been reported for intraindividual changes in anger, anxiety, and sympathy towards Ukrainians between 2022 and 2023 [38].

The present findings further show that anxiety, anger, and being moved were consistently associated with specific collective responses, ranging from outgroup help and ingroup defense to outgroup derogation and media mistrust.

Anxiety predicts derogation of Russians

People who felt anxious about the Ukrainian war were less inclined to defend their ingroup but more so to derogate the outgroup of Russian citizens. In contrast to previous findings, which found state anxiety to be predictive of refugee helping in Poland during the first three months after the Russian invasion [39], we did not observe any association between anxiety and solidarity towards Ukrainians. It's more like people who felt anxious about the war were also more prone to derogate the outgroup of Russian citizens, such as being suspicious of Russian people living in their country.

Anger predicts solidarity with Ukrainians, defense of the European ingroup, and derogation of Russians

Anger was involved in all group-based responses. People who felt angry about the Russian invasion reported more derogatory behavior towards Russians, similar to anxious people. However, the experience of anger also led people to be more supportive of solidaritybased action towards Ukrainians, and to more strongly defend their European ingroup, by expressing strength, loyalty and adherence to shared moral and democratic principles.

This confirms anger as a group-based emotion that is often elicited in intergroup situations, and that is associated with group-based responses. People experience anger when they perceive an intergroup conflict and thus experience a realistic or symbolic threat to their ingroup [40, 41] . Thereby, anger is always directed towards an outgroup that people deem responsible for the situation [42]. In line with this reasoning, we found that people who perceived the Ukrainian war to threaten Europe's safety, economy, and European core values experienced anger, which predicted support for defending the European liberal democratic order against Russia, and derogated citizens who ostensibly belonged to the Russian outgroup.

This corroborates previous findings showing that realistic and symbolic threat perceptions increase anti-immigrant prejudice through increased feelings of anger [43]. In addition, it provides first evidence that anger is also linked to ingroup support and value defense.

Moreover, we found anger to predict solidarity-based action (i.e., protesting for peace), supporting a basic finding of collective action research [37, 44, 45]. In the context of the Ukrainian war, anger might predict collective action intentions in particular, when the goal of solidarity-based action is protest for peace or protest against Russia [36, 38], whereas other emotions, such as being moved, rather predict collective action targeted at prosocial goals to support Ukraine [36].

Being moved predicts solidarity with Ukrainians and European ingroup defense

We found support for being moved as a collective approach emotion that binds (European) ingroup members together through solidarity-based action and ingroup defense. This is in line with previous findings showing a positive link between being moved and collective action participation in the context of societal crisis in general [10, 29], and collective peace protest during the Ukrainian war in particular [36]. The present study extends these findings, as we found first evidence that being moved negatively predicts palliative responses.

Being moved weakened derogation of the Russian outgroup and mistrust in public mainstream media. Together, the findings support the notion that being moved is tied to prosociality [33, 36], as solidarity was promoted while derogation was reduced, and to collective agency [29], as collective action and the demonstration of ingroup strength were enhanced while mistrust in media decreased.

In terms of a general threat and defense process [3, 24], this means that being moved reflects an approach-motivated emotional state that can be elicited in social crisis threats and that is directed towards direct and indirect resolution goals but not towards palliative efforts.

This underscores the potential of positive emotions, in particular being moved, to prevent the social divide in times of crisis threats. Therefore, the present results offer an avenue for future research, as previous research found symbolic threat perceptions to elicit primarily genuine negative emotions, such as anger, anxiety, guilt, resentment [16], or hate [43].

In addition to emotional states, such as being moved, threat perceptions may also fuel processes of motivated social cognition that account for solidarity [37]. For example, threat perceptions elicited by the Russian invasion in Ukraine increased identification with a common ingroup of Europeans [5] and with the Ukrainian outgroup [46], which in turn increased solidarity-based action [5]. To understand the variation in motivated collective threat responses, the present findings highlight the necessity to investigate different emotional processes together with cognitive processes of social categorization.

Limitations

The present findings are correlational in nature, and we could not draw any causal inferences from the reported path model. Therefore, mediational analyses to establish causal links between threat and response via emotional states were not appropriate here, and experimental or longitudinal designs are needed. However, we can conclude from the present findings that how people feel about the Ukrainian war has an impact on which collective responses they show. In addition, the path model sheds light on a broader picture: The interrelations between different threat perceptions, emotional states, and the full spectrum of collective responses, from outgroup help, ingroup defense, and outgroup derogation.

A second limitation is that our data were cross-sectional, collected across different samples over time. Therefore, the findings cannot speak for intraindividual changes in threat perceptions and collective responses over time. At the same time, the reported changes in the total amount of threat perceptions and responses from 2022 until 2025 should be interpreted with caution, as the samples were drawn from German-speaking European countries but were not matched regarding demographic factors, such as age, gender, and educational background.

Although we controlled for demographic indicators and for participants' experiences with military conflicts and refugee, and this did not change the reported results, this should be noted.

Finally, the generalizability of the findings can be limited. It is possible that our findings can be generalized to Europeans in West and Middle Europe, but not to countries in Eastern Europe. In Eastern Europe, European and national identities may be construed differently, thereby also increasing the relevance of other responses, such as conspiracies [7, 8], but also making prosociality and ingroup defense more important when the distance to the military conflict decreases.

Conclusion

Realistic and, in particular, symbolic threats to the European ingroup emerged during the war in Ukraine from the beginning in 2022 until 2025. They shaped emotional experiences in Europeans living in German-speaking countries, showing that emotional involvement lies at the heart of collective responses to threat. However, being anxious and angry about the war is a double-edged sword, as these emotions can strengthen the bond between Europeans as well as facilitating the social divide through outgroup derogation. At the same time, feeling moved by the war has the potential to counteract mistrust and derogation, alleviating the negative impact of intergroup conflicts on society. Investigating these different (emotional) mechanisms that foster ingroup agency and promote trust between members is necessary to better understand how societies can build collective resilience in times of crises.
